title: Free while living
hookLine: liberation is possible in this life, not only after

lines: A GATE AT THE END OF THE ROAD?
FREE WHILE YOU STILL HAVE A JOB.
cards: Liberation sounds like something at the end: a gate at the far side of a long road, a reward after the last breath. Yesterday's lesson could even be heard that way: this life is the turn, so the prize comes after.
But Sikh scripture has a phrase that turns that picture inside out. Two words, jivan mukat. Free while living.
Not free someday. Free while you still have a job, a family, a phone that won't stop buzzing. What could that look like on a weekday?

teach.b: Jivan means life, living. Mukat means freed, released. Together: one who is liberated while alive.

The Granth uses it of people walking around in the world, not only of souls after death. In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan says, in paraphrase: the one who takes the Lord's will to heart is called free while living.
To that person, joy and sorrow are alike; there is lasting bliss, and no separation. Notice what's missing. It doesn't say the free person has no sorrow.
It says sorrow and joy weigh the same. The storms still come. They just don't knock the person off the ground.

teach.h: FREE INSIDE, NOT FROM THE WORLD.
teach.b: Not from the world. Sikh life stays in it: family, work, langar, sangat. The freedom is from being pushed around inside, by ego, by fear, by the endless wanting more.
It ties the week together. Order and effort: you work, and accept the hukam. Deeds and grace: you do good and leave the door to the One.
A person who can actually live like that, here, is what jivan mukat names. If freedom came only after death, there'd be nothing to taste now.

teach.h: A TASTE, NOW, IN THIS LIFE.
teach.b: Jivan mukat says the taste is here, in this life, even in a hard week, even a moment at a time.

how: Sikhs recite Sukhmani Sahib, which describes the one who takes the Lord's will to heart as free while living, and Sikh teaching places that freedom inside family life, work and service, not apart from them.

o: liberated in this life, not only after death
released from this world at the moment of death
freed from all work and family duties

games.q: free while living: tap the pairs.

s: in Sikh scripture, liberation can only come after death
Sukhmani says the free person never feels sorrow
it says joy and sorrow are alike to them.
jivan mukat is a freedom lived inside family and work
free inside, not free from the world.

games.q: you want to be free while living. what do you do?
o: leave your family and work behind.
wait for freedom after your last breath.
take the will to heart, here, so joy and sorrow weigh the same.
games.why: Sukhmani: the one who takes the Lord's will to heart is called free while living.

practice: Let one good thing from this week sit in front of you, then set one hard thing beside it. Don't push the hard one away or hold on to the good one; let them sit side by side, the same weight, while you keep breathing.
If you pray, hold both as within the will; if you don't, notice the breath going on underneath both.

wordCard.voice: Free while living. Jivan mukat: liberated in this life, not only after it, where joy and sorrow weigh the same. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: jivan mukat, freed while living.

carryVoice: Your line: free now. The storms still come, and you stay standing. That's today, done.
